query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled slow‐cooling post‐heat treatment that induces fine, coherent precipitates clustering preferentially along grain boundaries to form a serrated morphology will enhance the load‐bearing integrity of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy while preserving its reversible caloric (magneto‐ and baro‐caloric) responses.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibiting large caloric responses but with coarse grain boundaries and a microstructure prone to intergranular cracking under load.
generation.intervention: Apply a brief high-temperature solution anneal followed by slow cooling (e.g., <5°C/min) in an inert atmosphere to promote controlled precipitation along grain boundaries, resulting in a serrated boundary morphology.
generation.conditions: The heat treatment is performed at a temperature just above the reversible transformation range (to avoid suppressing the caloric phase change) and then slowly cooled; subsequent operating conditions remain in the typical refrigeration regime under applied-field or pressure-field cycling at or near room temperature and under moderate mechanical loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, coherent precipitates along and within grain boundaries creates a serrated boundary architecture that deflects and blunts crack initiation and propagation without significantly altering the primary phase composition that enables the caloric effect.
generation.mechanism: Serrated grain boundaries improve crack resistance by distributing local strain and impeding intergranular crack propagation, while the coherency of the precipitates ensures that the lattice instabilities needed for the reversible caloric phase transformation are not impeded.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy should demonstrate a measurable improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., higher fracture toughness and ductility under tensile testing) with caloric response parameters (such as entropy and adiabatic temperature changes) that remain within ±10% of those of the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which offers strong caloric performance but suffers from poor load-bearing integrity, exemplified by premature cracking under operational loading.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under refrigeration operating conditions (moderate fields and pressures near room temperature) and within mechanical load regimes typical of refrigeration device components; performance under extreme mechanical or thermal cycling remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines findings from studies where controlled thermal treatments induced serrated grain boundaries that improved ductility and toughness (e.g., evidence from PMC9848264 and related reports) with strategies that yield coherent precipitates (as seen with Zr additions in PMC8539796). However, applying such processing to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and ensuring that the precipitates are benign with respect to the reversible caloric phase change is untested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples – one set subject to the proposed slow-cooling heat treatment and one set processed via conventional rapid quenching. Characterize the microstructures using electron microscopy to confirm the presence or absence of serrated grain boundaries. Then, subject both sample sets to identical mechanical testing (tensile and fracture toughness) and caloric performance evaluation under applied magnetic/pressure fields.
measurements: Quantitative metrics of fracture toughness and tensile ductility
Caloric performance indicators such as isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change
Electron microscopy images confirming grain boundary morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not exhibit at least a 15% improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., fracture toughness or ductility) or if their caloric response is degraded by more than 10% compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe effect of Zr addition on the melting temperature of the CoCrFeMnNi High Entropy Alloy (HEA), known as the “Cantor’s Alloy”, is investigated, together with its micro-structure, mechanical properties and thermomechanical recrystallization process. The base and Zr-modified alloys are obtained by vacuum induction melting of mechanically pre-alloyed powders. Raw materials are then cold rolled and annealed. recrystallization occurred during the heat treatment of the cold-rolled HEA. The alloys are characterized by X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, thermal analyses, mechanical spectroscopy and indentation measures. The main advantages of Zr addition are: (1) a fast vacuum induction melting process; (2) the lower melting temperature, due to Zr eutectics formation with all the Cantor’s alloy elements; (3) the good chemical alloy homogeneity; and (4) the mechanical properties improvement of re-crystallized grains with a coherent structure. The crystallographic lattice of both alloys results in FCC. ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
